name: bruno-simon.com
object_type: Portfolio — a personal creative-developer portfolio, but an atypical one: it is simultaneously a marketing surface for the owner's commercial product (the Three.js Journey course) and a public tech demo / teaching artifact for Three.js + TSL/WebGPU. It is not a job-application document in any conventional sense.
format_genre: 3D/game. A single fullscreen WebGL/WebGPU canvas containing a drivable low-poly diorama world; the visitor steers a jeep with WASD/arrows (or touch/gamepad) through themed 'areas' to reach content. There is no scroll page underneath it and no document fallback. The current live build is the 2025/2026 rewrite (repo `folio-2025`), which adds a game loop with achievements, a timed race circuit, weather/day-night cycles, and light multiplayer features on top of the drivable-world concept established in the 2019 version.
intent_audience: Personal brand / authority-building first, with a commercial funnel second. It is explicitly NOT job-seeking: there is no resume, no 'hire me', no availability statement, no contact form. The primary conversion is credibility in the creative-dev/WebGL industry (agency and freelance inbound comes from reputation, not from a CTA), and the strongest on-site link is to the paid Three.js Journey course, which is also listed as the first 'project'. Secondary audience: the Three.js learner community, served via the open-source repo, YouTube devlogs, and a public Discord.
seniority_stage: Senior specialist / founder. Bruno Simon is a well-known WebGL/Three.js creative developer (ex Immersive Garden, ex Hervé Studio, freelance) who now runs Three.js Journey as a product business. 'Good' for this item means industry-leading craft and technical novelty, not legibility to a recruiter — the site is judged by peers and awards juries, and it optimises accordingly.
language_i18n: English only. `<html lang="en">`, all UI copy and achievement text in English. No EN/other toggle. Country flags appear only as a cosmetic selector in the 'Whispers' visitor-message feature, not as a language switch. Owner is French; the site does not offer French.
owner_role: Bruno Simon — French creative developer, self-described on site as 'a creative developer (mostly for the web)'. WebGL/Three.js specialist; creator and instructor of the Three.js Journey course; previously WebGL/front-end developer at Immersive Garden and Hervé Studio (both credited in the project metadata). Signs the colophon simply '— Bruno'.
sections_present: Present, but all as physical 'areas' in the 3D world rather than nav items: (1) About — a 'Welcome!' panel with a two-sentence intro; (2) Projects — the ProjectsArea gallery of 8 client works; (3) Lab — 13 personal WebGL experiments, a second projects tier; (4) Career — a drivable timeline area with years starting at 2008 and role/employer text carved into 3D stones (the Experience section); (5) Behind the Scene — a colophon documenting the full stack, source code, licence and music credits; (6) Social — an in-world shrine cluster of contact/social links; (7) Discord — public server + direct-message modal. ABSENT: Resume/CV (no PDF, no inline CV), Skills list (skills are demonstrated, never enumerated), Blog (the YouTube devlog playlist is the substitute), Testimonials. Extra non-portfolio sections that exist purely as engagement mechanics: Achievements (38 entries with a playtime counter and cosmetic reward tiers), Circuit (timed race with a daily top-10 leaderboard), Whispers (visitor-left 30-character messages, max 30 shown), plus joke areas (Bowling, Toilet, Cookie, Easter, Altar, Time Machine).
nav_pattern: Single page, single canvas, no routes and no URL changes per section — navigation is spatial. You drive to content. Supporting affordances: a minimal HUD of icon buttons (home, map, settings, controls, achievements, circuit, whispers, behind-the-scene), an `M` map overlay, and an `R`/'I'm stuck!' respawn that teleports you to the nearest checkpoint. Areas open HTML panels when the car enters their bounding volume. There is no menu that lists the sections as text links, so section discovery is exploratory and non-guaranteed.
visual_style: Stylized low-poly game diorama — 'tiny and colourful architecture, very flat but with slightly rounded edges' (the owner credits Gustavo Henrique as the reference). Isometric-ish chase camera over a cartoon island. Design-trend alignment: it deliberately sits outside the 2D web-design trend cycle — no bento grid, no neo-brutalism, no glassmorphism, no kinetic typography. Its 'trend' is the immersive-WebGL/awards-site genre, and within that it pushes the current frontier (WebGPU via Three.js TSL, GPU particles, volumetric weather, dynamic day/night and seasons). A defining choice in the 2025 rewrite is diegetic UI: menus and labels were moved out of HTML into 3D models inside the world wherever possible, so the interface is part of the scenery rather than an overlay. Only a small residual HTML layer (panels, HUD icons) remains.
color_typography: Fixed dark art direction — deep plum/near-black surfaces (#251f2b, #1d1721) with warm accents: pale pink (#ffceca), coral (#ff6a7c), lime (#d5ff95), amber (#ffc67b). Type: Amatic SC (condensed hand-drawn display, headings) paired with Nunito (rounded sans, body), both from Google Fonts with `display=block`; Pally is also referenced for some UI weights. No light/dark mode toggle and no `prefers-color-scheme` handling anywhere in the CSS — the world itself supplies the light/dark variation through its day/night cycle.
motion: Motion is the product, not a decoration: continuous real-time physics simulation (Rapier3D), a camera that constantly follows and reframes, GSAP tweens for every panel reveal and label wipe, plus rain, snow, lightning, wind and tornado effects. `prefers-reduced-motion` is not respected — the string appears zero times in either the shipped CSS or the ~4.9 MB JS bundle. The only user-side mitigations are a Quality toggle (drops effects/shadow resolution) and an Audio mute; neither stops camera or world motion. For a motion-sensitive visitor the site has no usable mode.
responsiveness_mobile: It does not degrade into a document on small screens — it stays a game and swaps the input model instead. A dedicated touch scheme is documented in-site: one finger to drive, two fingers for camera/zoom, tap the car to jump; a gamepad scheme is also supported. A mobile quality preset automatically disables expensive effects and reduces shadow resolution, and the 2019 version already clamped pixel ratio and dropped blur for phones. HN reports say the 2026 build is genuinely smooth on iOS Safari and Android. The real cost is not layout but energy and legibility: sustained GPU load (reports of ~100% CPU and 60–70 W draw on laptops, plus isolated Firefox/MacBook crashes), and the fact that a phone user who wants to know what Bruno has built must drive to it — nothing is scannable, copy-pasteable, or reachable in one screenful. There is no `<noscript>` and no text-only route, so a device without WebGL gets nothing.
framework_hosting: No site generator and no UI framework — hand-written vanilla ES modules bundled by Vite 7, with Stylus for the thin HTML/CSS layer. Rendering: Three.js r183 imported as `three/webgpu` with TSL (Three.js Shading Language), which lets the same shader code run on WebGPU where available and fall back to WebGL — the renderer is user-switchable in the Options panel. Physics: @dimforge/rapier3d (WASM, loaded via vite-plugin-wasm + top-level-await). Animation: GSAP. Audio: Howler.js. Debug: Tweakpane + stats-gl. Asset pipeline: everything modelled in Blender (naming conventions in the .blend drive runtime behaviour), exported to glTF, compressed with gltf-transform (Draco) and KTX-Software to GPU texture formats (ETC1S/UASTC), via a custom `npm run compress` script. Hosting: self-hosted, not a JAMstack host — nginx 1.24 on Ubuntu at a Hostinger VPS in Paris (srv740865.hstgr.cloud, AS47583), serving a plain static `dist/` with no CDN or edge-cache headers visible. Custom domain is the owner's own name on a .com — a strong personal-brand TLD signal. A separate private Node server backs the multiplayer features (whispers, cookie counter, daily leaderboard); its source is deliberately withheld and it was offline at the time of research, with the client degrading gracefully to 'Server currently offline'.
performance_a11y: Performance: heavy by design and honest about it. The entry HTML is 58.8 KB, CSS 6.5 KB compressed, but the single JS bundle is ~1.03 MB compressed / 4.86 MB raw, before any of the GLB models, KTX texture atlases and music tracks stream in — the repo carries roughly 750 MB of source assets, and the shipped payload is orders of magnitude above a normal portfolio (the far leaner 2019 version was already 2.8 MB total). Runtime cost is sustained rather than one-off: continuous physics + render loop, with community reports of near-100% CPU and 60–70 W power draw on laptops and occasional Firefox crashes, against 'perfectly smooth' on an M3 MacBook Air. First meaningful interaction is gated behind a loading sequence. Accessibility: effectively absent, and this is the site's clearest trade-off. Zero `aria-*` attributes in the document, no `<h1>` at all, only 3 `alt` attributes across 41 buttons, no skip link, no focus-visible strategy, no `prefers-reduced-motion`, no `<noscript>`, no reduced/text mode. Keyboard input exists but drives a vehicle rather than traversing content, so a screen-reader or keyboard-only user cannot reach the project list. Positives are thin but real: `lang="en"` is set, contrast within the HTML panels is high, and the panel copy (welcome text, controls, behind-the-scene colophon) is present as real text in the served HTML, so a crawler sees something. There is no robots.txt and no sitemap.xml (both 404).
analytics_instrumentation: Google Analytics 4 only — `gtag.js` with measurement ID G-JMSN30BQ5J, loaded async in the head. No Plausible, Umami, Vercel Analytics, Fathom, or session-replay tooling. In-world engagement telemetry is client-side and local (achievement progress, playtime counter) plus the private multiplayer server for whispers/leaderboard.
project_presentation:
Two clearly separated tiers, both presented as drivable outdoor galleries rather than cards.

TIER 1 — ProjectsArea (client work, 8 entries). Each project is a large ground-mounted board carrying a slideshow of KTX-compressed screenshots, a 3D-typeset title, structured metadata rendered in-world (`role`, `at` = studio, `with` = collaborators), and award badges drawn from a fixed vocabulary of awwwards / FWA / CSSDA. Interacting opens the project's live production URL in a new tab. The set: Three.js Journey (threejs-journey.com, role developer+trainer, FWA); Bonhomme | 10 ans (anniversary.bonhommeparis.com, awwwards+FWA); Madbox (madbox.io, at Hervé Studio, awwwards); Luni (luni.app, at Hervé Studio, awwwards+FWA); Scout (scout-omega.vercel.app, at Hervé Studio); Prior Holdings (prior.co.jp, at Immersive Garden, awwwards+CSSDA+FWA); Orano (orano.group, at Immersive Garden, awwwards+CSSDA+FWA); Citrix/Redbull (at Immersive Garden, awwwards+CSSDA+FWA). One entry, Chartogne-Taillet, is commented out in the source.

TIER 2 — LabArea (13 personal experiments), presented the same way but lighter: title + single image + live link. Black Hole, Infinite World, My Room in 3D, Particles System, Stylized Low Poly, Holographic Terrain, Woodkid Volcano Robot, Bounce Friday, VFX Flames, VFX Tornado, DOOM Portal, Organic Sphere, Attractors.

Live-demo availability is effectively 100% — every single entry in both tiers resolves to a working hosted experience. Hosts: Vercel for the personal lab experiments (the dominant pattern, e.g. infinite-world.vercel.app, my-room-in-3d.vercel.app), threejs.org/examples for the three TSL demos that were upstreamed into Three.js itself, threejs-journey.com for course apps, and client production domains for agency work.

What is deliberately missing: no per-project case-study page, no problem/approach/outcome narrative, no tech-stack tags, no GitHub repo link per project, no dates. Credibility is carried entirely by (a) the award badges, (b) the named studio/collaborator, and (c) the live site itself. The three Three.js-repo demos are an unusually strong signal — upstream contributions to the library the whole portfolio is built on.
resume_integration_mode: None of the four modes. There is no PDF download, no inline HTML CV, and nothing ATS-parseable — a resume parser fed this URL would extract almost nothing. The functional substitute is the CareerArea: a drivable 3D timeline whose year counter starts at 2008 and advances as you move forward, with employer/role text baked into stone geometry and revealed by a shader wipe as you approach. Employment history is therefore visible but not extractable, not copyable, and not indexable. LinkedIn (linked from the Social area) carries the machine-readable version.
proof_verifiability: Reasonably strong for a site with zero prose claims, because the proof mechanism is delegation rather than assertion. Every project links to the live production site, which is self-verifying. Every project carries third-party award badges (awwwards / FWA / CSSDA) and names the agency and the collaborators involved, so claims are attributable and checkable by someone in the industry. Role honesty is notable: Bruno labels himself 'WebGL developer' on agency work rather than claiming the whole build. The site's own claim — 'I can build this' — is verified by the MIT-licensed source of the site itself, including the Blender files. Weaknesses: award badges are icons, not hyperlinks to the award pages, so verification requires a manual search [uncertain]; and the site itself never states dates, so 'when' is unverifiable on-site. The site's own external validation (awwwards Site of the Year for the 2019 version; awwwards Site of the Day at 8.11 on 2026-01-21 for the current build) is documented off-site, not claimed on-site.
quantified_impact: Effectively zero conventional metrics. There are no user counts, no revenue figures, no latency/accuracy/cost-saved numbers, no 'increased conversions by X%' — the site never argues in business terms at all. Instead the quantification is gamified and self-referential: a live playtime counter (e.g. '2h 30min 15s'), 38 achievements with explicit numeric thresholds (visit all 13 areas, view all 8 projects, view all 13 lab items, accept 1/10/100/1000 cookies), cosmetic reward tiers (red, orange, white, black, flames, abyssal), a daily top-10 race leaderboard, and a 30-slot visitor whisper wall. This is a deliberate inversion: the metric shown is the visitor's engagement, not the owner's impact. The hard impact numbers exist only in off-site case studies — the 2019 version drew ~160,000 visits in its first week at 2.8 MB total weight and ~54 s average session, and is commonly cited at 400,000+ visits [uncertain]; the 2025/2026 rebuild took a little over a year of work, documented in a full YouTube devlog series across 930 commits.
content_freshness: Very fresh, and freshness is structurally demonstrated rather than stated. The entire site was rebuilt and relaunched around the end of 2025 (repo `folio-2025` created 2024-10-12, 930 commits); the served index.html carries Last-Modified 2026-04-07 and the repo's last push is the same day. It won awwwards SOTD on 2026-01-21 and was on the Hacker News front page shortly after launch. The YouTube devlog series functions as an ongoing 'currently working on' signal. There is no explicit now/status widget on the site, and one small staleness tell is visible to visitors: the multiplayer backend was showing 'Server currently offline. Scores can't be saved.' at time of research, which makes two of the engagement features inert. Note also that the client project list has not grown much — the freshness is in the vessel, not the work shown.
writing_tone: Playful, warm, first-person and disarmingly modest — the opposite of the technical bravado the build implies. The whole About section is two sentences: 'My name is Bruno Simon, and I'm a creative developer (mostly for the web). This is my portfolio. Please drive around to learn more about me and discover the many secrets of this world. And don't break anything!' The colophon opens 'Thank you for visiting my portfolio!' and signs off '— Bruno'. Humour is layered in everywhere: achievement names like 'I'm going on an adventure!', 'But can you fix the wifi?', 'Wake & bake', 'It's About Sending A Message'; joke areas (a toilet, a bowling alley); and an ASCII-art easter egg in the browser console addressed to 'you sneaky developer'. Generosity is a consistent note — the code is MIT, the Blender files are included, the commissioned music was released CC0, and the credits section names mrdoob and sunag before it names anything of Bruno's own.
standout_features:
Ranked by how borrowable they are for a conventional portfolio on a normal time budget.

CHEAP AND WORTH STEALING:
1. Award/proof badges as first-class project metadata — a tiny data-model choice (`distinctions: ['awwwards','fwa','cssda']`) that converts each project card from a claim into a citation. Trivially portable to any card grid.
2. Honest role attribution per project (`role`, `at`, `with`) — 'WebGL developer at Immersive Garden, with Rémi Tran' reads as more credible than an implied solo build, and costs three extra strings per entry.
3. Two-tier project taxonomy: 8 curated client projects vs 13 quick lab experiments, visually and spatially separated. Solves the 'do I include the small stuff?' problem without diluting the headline work.
4. Every single item links to a working live demo, with Vercel as the default host for experiments. No dead links, no 'screenshots only'.
5. A real 'Behind the Scene' colophon that names the stack, links the source, credits every dependency and contributor, and states the licence. It is the cheapest possible authenticity signal and doubles as a teaching artifact.
6. Console easter egg with ASCII art plus all contact details — costs ten minutes and is aimed squarely at the exact audience that opens devtools.
7. Voice: two-sentence About, humour throughout, credit given to others before self. Zero engineering cost, large differentiation.

EXPENSIVE — ADMIRE, DO NOT COPY:
8. The drivable world itself, diegetic 3D UI (menus modelled in Blender rather than HTML), physics-driven interaction, day/night + seasonal weather, commissioned CC0 soundtrack.
9. The engagement layer: 38 achievements with reward tiers, a timed race circuit with a daily leaderboard, and a visitor 'whispers' message wall — light multiplayer that turns a portfolio into a place people return to. Note the cost: it requires a private backend, and when that backend is down the features visibly break.
10. Career as a drivable timeline (year counter driven by the player's z-position, role text revealed by shader wipe) — a genuinely novel Experience section, at maybe 100x the cost of a `<ul>`.
11. Building the portfolio as a public year-long devlog series on YouTube — the process became a bigger distribution asset than the artifact.
12. Shipping on WebGPU-via-TSL with automatic WebGL fallback and a user-facing renderer switch — the portfolio doubles as a credible demo of the thing he teaches.

THE STRUCTURAL LESSON: the site works because the medium IS the claim. A WebGL specialist proving WebGL mastery has perfect message-medium fit, and the accessibility/performance/legibility costs are the price he can afford to pay because his audience is peers and juries, not recruiters or ATS. For a software engineer whose claim is not 'I make 3D experiences', the same trade would be pure cost — which is exactly why this belongs in the research set as an ROI ceiling and contrast point, not a template.
originality_vs_template: Fully custom, zero template lineage — hand-written vanilla JS with no UI framework, a bespoke Blender-to-runtime asset pipeline, and a custom game loop. It is the origin point of the lineage rather than a member of it: `folio-2019` has ~4.7k stars and ~1,029 forks and spawned an entire genre of imitation portfolios, tutorial series ('Let's Recreate Bruno Simon's Portfolio Using React Three Fiber'), and DEV/Medium clone write-ups; `folio-2025` already has ~1.6k stars and 282 forks. Anyone shipping a drivable-car portfolio today is, knowingly or not, forking this.
source_available: Yes, and unusually completely — github.com/brunosimon/folio-2025 under MIT, ~1.6k stars / 282 forks / 930 commits, including the Blender source files for the entire world, not just the compiled glTF. The previous generation, github.com/brunosimon/folio-2019, remains public too (~4.7k stars). The commissioned soundtrack was additionally released under CC0 with a direct download link. One deliberate carve-out, stated plainly on the site: the multiplayer server code is withheld 'for security reasons', and the client is built to work without it. This is a strong dogfooding/credibility signal — the site is simultaneously the portfolio, the proof, and the teaching material for his paid course.
contact_methods: No contact form, no email-capture, no 'hire me' CTA anywhere. Contact lives in a dedicated SocialArea where each channel is a physical 3D shrine you drive into: X (@bruno_simon), Bluesky, YouTube (@BrunoSimon), Mail (mailto: link), Twitch (bruno_simon_dev), GitHub (brunosimon), LinkedIn (in/simonbruno77), and Discord — the last opening a modal offering both a public community server ('come hang out with the community, show us your projects and ask us anything') and a direct-message link, with the candid caveat 'I try to answer everyone, but it might take a while.' Placement is spatial rather than persistent: unlike a normal portfolio there is no header or footer social row, so contact is only reachable by exploring — a real discoverability cost accepted in exchange for immersion. The same full list is duplicated in the browser-console easter egg, which is the only place it can be copy-pasted.
pii_exposure: One notable exposure: a personal Gmail address, simon.bruno.77@gmail.com, is shipped in cleartext in three places — the `sources/data/social.js` file in the public repo, the shipped JS bundle behind the in-world Mail shrine's mailto link, and the browser-console easter egg. It is unobfuscated and trivially scrapeable. No phone number, no postal address, no employer-internal detail, and no personal photo of the owner appears on the site. Real name is intentionally public (it is the brand and the domain). Visitor-side privacy note: Google Analytics 4 runs with no cookie/consent banner, and the 'Whispers' feature accepts and displays visitor-submitted text (30-char cap, one per user, moderation for slurs stated) alongside a self-selected country flag.
